label: Level of fame impact
summary: The game concept Level of Fame Impact: makes the modifiers a character gets from their current level of fame stronger or weaker.
details: In a text, `[prestige_level_impact|E]` shows "Level of Fame Impact" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the name of the modifier that changes this impact.

label: Level of fame
summary: The plural name of the game concept Level of Fame: a character's general reputation.
details: In a text, `[prestige_levels|E]` shows "Levels of Fame" linked to the Level of Fame explanation. Vanilla uses it in effect texts that say how many levels were gained or lost.

label: Prestige
summary: The adjective form of the game concept Prestige ("Prestigious"), linked to the Prestige explanation.
details: In a text, `[prestigious|E]` shows "Prestigious" linked to the Prestige explanation. Vanilla uses it in decision and event texts, for example a hunt becoming less prestigious.

label: Prevented murder
summary: The game concept Prevented Murder: a murder scheme that fails at the last moment because of something in the target's life.
details: In a text, `[prevented_murder|E]` shows "Prevented Murder" linked to the concept's explanation. It is rare and overrides the scheme's success chance; examples are a bodyguard, a food taster, a shieldmaiden or a loyal pet stepping in. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Prevented murder
summary: The verb form of the game concept Prevented Murder ("Prevent"), linked to the Prevented Murder explanation.
details: In a text, `[prevented_murder_prevent|E]` shows "Prevent" linked to the Prevented Murder explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a text about preventing one murder scheme against each dynasty member.

label: Primary heir
summary: The game concept Primary Heir: the character who inherits a ruler's primary title when the ruler dies.
details: In a text, `[primary_heir|E]` shows "Primary Heir" linked to the concept's explanation. This is usually, but not always, the same character as the player heir. Vanilla uses it in many texts, such as the decision to choose a primary heir.

label: Primary heir
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Primary Heir ("Primary Heir's"), linked to its explanation.
details: In a text, `[primary_heir_possessive|E]` shows "Primary Heir's" linked to the Primary Heir explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a message filter about the heir's marriage ending.

label: Primary heir
summary: The plural name of the game concept Primary Heir: the characters who inherit their rulers' primary titles.
details: In a text, `[primary_heirs|E]` shows "Primary Heirs" linked to the Primary Heir explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a coronation activity text.

label: Primary spouse
summary: The game concept Primary Spouse: in faiths that allow several spouses, the one spouse a ruler picks as their main one.
details: In a text, `[primary_spouse|E]` shows "Primary Spouse" linked to the concept's explanation. The primary spouse has higher fertility with the ruler and a better opinion of them, and can sit on their council. Vanilla uses it in vassal stance and diarchy texts.

label: Primary title
summary: The game concept Primary Title: a ruler's highest-ranked title, the one they are most identified with.
details: In a text, `[primary_title|E]` shows "Primary Title" linked to the concept's explanation. It decides the ruler's coat of arms and the name of their realm; a ruler with several titles of the same tier can choose which one it is.

label: Primary title
summary: The plural name of the game concept Primary Title: rulers' highest-ranked titles, the ones they are most identified with.
details: In a text, `[primary_titles|E]` shows "Primary Titles" linked to the Primary Title explanation. Vanilla uses it in interaction texts, for example that only a governor's primary titles can be revoked.

label: Prince-elector
summary: The game concept Prince-Elector: one of the seven electors who choose the heir to the empire together with the emperor under princely elective succession.
details: In a text, `[prince_elector|E]` shows "Prince-Elector" linked to the concept's explanation. Holders of seven preferred titles, chosen when the empire is created, get the seats first. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Prince-elector
summary: The plural name of the game concept Prince-Elector: the seven electors who choose the heir to the empire together with the emperor.
details: In a text, `[prince_electors|E]` shows "Prince-Electors" linked to the Prince-Elector explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts about how the electors are selected.

label: Prison
summary: The game concept Prison: where landed rulers keep their prisoners, in a dungeon or under house arrest.
details: In a text, `[prison|E]` shows "Prison" linked to the concept's explanation. Characters can be captured in battle or after a siege, and anyone in one's own realm can be arrested, though without a crime that counts as tyranny. Prisoners can be executed, tortured, ransomed and more; a camp keeps them in its stockade.

label: Prison
summary: A name of the game concept Prison ("Prisoner"), linked to the Prison explanation.
details: In a text, `[prisoner|E]` shows "Prisoner" linked to the Prison explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts, for example the concept texts about prisoners and the ransom action.

label: Prisoner of war
summary: The game concept Prisoner of War: a prisoner taken in a war who is not important enough to give the captors war score.
details: In a text, `[prisoner_of_war|E]` shows "Prisoner of War" linked to the concept's explanation. Valuable prisoners are a different group: they are released when the war ends, but they can still be ransomed. Vanilla uses it in message filter texts about prisoners taken in battles and sieges.

label: Prison
summary: A plural name of the game concept Prison ("Prisoners"), linked to the Prison explanation.
details: In a text, `[prisoners|E]` shows "Prisoners" linked to the Prison explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts.

label: Prisoner of war
summary: The plural name of the game concept Prisoner of War: prisoners taken in a war who are not important enough to give war score.
details: In a text, `[prisoners_of_war|E]` shows "Prisoners of War" linked to the Prisoner of War explanation. Vanilla uses it in the concept text about valuable prisoners.

label: Prison
summary: The plural name of the game concept Prison ("Prisons"), linked to the Prison explanation.
details: In a text, `[prisons|E]` shows "Prisons" linked to the Prison explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Privation
summary: The game concept Privation: the hardship a travelling camp suffers when its provisions run low or out.
details: In a text, `[privation|E]` shows "Privation" linked to the concept's explanation. A camp that stays put can just about feed itself, but while travelling it lives on its provisions. As they run low, followers lose opinion of their leader, and it can escalate to starvation and death.

label: Prize
summary: The game concept Prize: an artifact given to the winner of a tournament contest that has a single winner.
details: In a text, `[prize|E]` shows "Prize" linked to the concept's explanation. How good the prize is depends on the host's chosen options and on the era. Vanilla uses it in tournament texts.

label: Prize
summary: The plural name of the game concept Prize: artifacts given to the winners of single-winner tournament contests.
details: In a text, `[prizes|E]` shows "Prizes" linked to the Prize explanation. Vanilla uses it in tournament concept texts.

label: Progress to victory
summary: The game concept Progress to Victory: how likely a character is to win a contest compared with the other contestants.
details: In a text, `[progress_to_victory|E]` shows "Progress to Victory" linked to the concept's explanation. It rests on skills, health and traits, for example a strong giant does well in wrestling. A minimum value guarantees qualifying for a contest; visiting locales can improve it or hurt rivals.

label: Prohibited
summary: The verb form of the game concept Prohibited ("Prohibit"), the tenet status for a tenet or doctrine a rite forbids.
details: In a text, `[prohibit_tenet_status|E]` shows "Prohibit" linked to the Prohibited explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the text for choosing a core tenet to prohibit within a faith.

label: Prohibited
summary: The game concept Prohibited: the tenet status meaning a rite expressly forbids a core tenet or doctrine.
details: In a text, `[prohibited_tenet_status|E]` shows "Prohibited" linked to the concept's explanation. A character of that rite who takes the tenet as a personal tenet keeps it secret, and a rite that makes prohibited tenets core tenets drifts much further from its faith (becomes more divergent).

label: Project
summary: The game concept Project: what an inspired character undertakes with a sponsor's help, usually making an artifact.
details: In a text, `[project|E]` shows "Project" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in decision texts about commissioning artifacts.

label: Promote culture
summary: The game concept Promote Culture: the steward's council task that changes a county's culture to its ruler's.
details: In a text, `[promote_culture|E]` shows "Promote Culture" (the task's own name) linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in culture texts, for example about hybrid cultures spreading faster.

label: Celebrate other cultures decision
summary: The game concept Celebrate Other Cultures Decision: a decision that improves the realm's counties of other cultures that are well accepted.
details: In a text, `[promote_other_culture_development_decision|E]` shows "Celebrate Other Cultures Decision" linked to the concept's explanation. It helps counties whose culture has at least 75% cultural acceptance with development, control, building costs and defensive advantage, and gives prestige and levies. Its gold cost grows with the number of such counties.

label: Promoted legend
summary: The game concept Promoted Legend: a legend owned by another ruler that promoters back with a monthly payment to share its bonuses.
details: In a text, `[promoted_legend|E]` shows "Promoted Legend" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in court position and message texts about others promoting one's legend.

label: Promote cultural acceptance
summary: A name of the game concept Promote Cultural Acceptance ("Promoting Acceptance"): the steward's council task that raises acceptance between a culture and the ruler's.
details: In a text, `[promoting_cultural_acceptance|E]` shows "Promoting Acceptance" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the culture window, to say a character is doing this task.

label: Promoted legend
summary: A verb form of the game concept Promoted Legend ("Promoting"), linked to the Promoted Legend explanation.
details: In a text, `[promoting_legend|E]` shows "Promoting" linked to the Promoted Legend explanation. Vanilla uses it in legend texts, for example a warning that the character already promotes a legend.

label: Prosperity decree
summary: The game concept Prosperity Decree: a mandala ruler's decree that pushes all subjects towards building up their lands.
details: In a text, `[prosperity_decree|E]` shows "Prosperity" linked to the concept's explanation. The effort goes into development, buildings, wealth and personal relations. Vanilla uses it in mandala decision texts.

label: Province
summary: The game concept Province: a title held by a governor in an administrative realm.
details: In a text, `[province|E]` shows "Province" linked to the concept's explanation. Each province has a province administration that strongly affects what it gives. Many vanilla texts write `province` as a saved scope instead (`[province.GetName]`), which is a different thing.

label: Province administration
summary: The game concept Province Administration: the specialisation of a province in an administrative realm, set by the liege and the governor.
details: In a text, `[province_administration|E]` shows "Province Administration" linked to the concept's explanation. A province can have only one at a time. Vanilla uses it in subject contract texts.

label: Province administration
summary: The short name of the game concept Province Administration ("Administration"), linked to its explanation.
details: In a text, `[province_administration_short|E]` shows "Administration" linked to the Province Administration explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts about celestial province types.

label: Province administration
summary: The plural name of the game concept Province Administration: the specialisations of provinces in an administrative realm.
details: In a text, `[province_administrations|E]` shows "Province Administrations" linked to the Province Administration explanation. Vanilla uses it in a few concept texts.

label: Province
summary: The plural name of the game concept Province: titles held by governors in an administrative realm.
details: In a text, `[provinces|E]` shows "Provinces" linked to the Province explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts about province types.

label: Province
summary: The adjective form of the game concept Province ("Provincial"), linked to the Province explanation.
details: In a text, `[provincial|E]` shows "Provincial" linked to the Province explanation. Vanilla uses it in law texts such as provincial war declaration.

label: Provincial army
summary: The plural name of the game concept Provincial Army: armies raised and kept by governors in administrative realms.
details: In a text, `[provincial_armies|E]` shows "Provincial Armies" linked to the Provincial Army explanation. Vanilla uses it in law and other texts.

label: Provincial army
summary: The game concept Provincial Army: an army raised and kept by a governor in a realm with an administrative government.
details: In a text, `[provincial_army|E]` shows "Provincial Army" linked to the concept's explanation. It consists only of title men-at-arms, whose strength depends on the governor's efficiency. The liege can spend influence to take control of it, and governors can sometimes borrow troops from their peers.

label: Provincial examination
summary: The game concept Provincial Examination: the second level of the imperial examinations, taken through the local examination activity.
details: In a text, `[provincial_examination|E]` shows "Provincial Examination" linked to the concept's explanation. Passing it gives a modifier, which the concept text shows with its effects. Vanilla uses it in merit level texts.

label: Provincial examination
summary: The icon form of the game concept Provincial Examination: it shows the provincial exam icon, linked to the explanation.
details: The concept text for this name is the provincial exam icon. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Provisions
summary: The singular name of the game concept Provisions ("Provision"), linked to the Provisions explanation.
details: In a text, `[provision|E]` shows "Provision" linked to the Provisions explanation. Vanilla uses it in perk, decision event and men-at-arms texts about provision costs.

label: Provisions
summary: The game concept Provisions: the food, water and shelter a camp has to live on.
details: In a text, `[provisions|E]` shows "Provisions" linked to the concept's explanation. A camp uses them up while moving; how fast depends on its men-at-arms, the terrain and its officers. When they run low, followers suffer privation.

label: Provisions
summary: The icon form of the game concept Provisions: it shows the provisions icon instead of a word.
details: The concept text for this name is the provisions icon. Vanilla writes `[provisions_i]` without `|E`, which shows only the icon, in front of amounts of provisions.

label: Prowess skill
summary: The short name of the game concept Prowess Skill ("Prowess"): the skill for a character's ability in personal combat.
details: In a text, `[prowess|E]` shows "Prowess" linked to the Prowess Skill explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts.

label: Prowess skill
summary: The icon form of the game concept Prowess Skill: it shows the prowess skill icon instead of a word.
details: The concept text for this name is the prowess skill icon. Vanilla writes `[prowess_i]` in front of the word, as in "[prowess_i][prowess_skill|E]".

label: Prowess skill
summary: The game concept Prowess Skill: the skill for a character's ability in personal combat.
details: In a text, `[prowess_skill|E]` shows "Prowess Skill" linked to the concept's explanation. High prowess helps a character survive and do well as a knight in battle and in duels; each point gives a knight damage and toughness (amounts from the `NCombat` defines).

label: Puppet
summary: The game concept Puppet: a character controlled by a puppeteer, who can take special actions through them.
details: In a text, `[puppet|E]` shows "Puppet" linked to the concept's explanation. For example, a clerical puppet can ask for clerical titles or an excommunication for the puppeteer, and an external ruler puppet can be made to release tributaries, grant independence or divorce. The puppet type decides the actions.

label: Puppet type
summary: The game concept Puppet Type: the type every puppet has, which decides the actions they can take for their puppeteer.
details: In a text, `[puppet_type|E]` shows "Puppet Type" linked to the concept's explanation. Most actions are shared, but each type has some of its own. A puppeteer can have only one puppet of each type.

label: Puppet type
summary: The plural name of the game concept Puppet Type: the types of puppet, which decide the actions each can take.
details: In a text, `[puppet_types|E]` shows "Puppet Types" linked to the Puppet Type explanation. Vanilla uses it in tutorial texts.

label: Puppet
summary: The adjective form of the game concept Puppet ("Puppeted"), linked to the Puppet explanation.
details: In a text, `[puppeted|E]` shows "Puppeted" linked to the Puppet explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a list of conditions.

label: Puppeteer
summary: The game concept Puppeteer: a character who controls one or more puppets.
details: In a text, `[puppeteer|E]` shows "Puppeteer" linked to the concept's explanation. Through their puppets a puppeteer has powers beyond their own position, such as the clergy's influence or a foreign realm's authority.

label: Puppeteer
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Puppeteer ("Puppeteer's"), linked to the Puppeteer explanation.
details: In a text, `[puppeteer_possessive|E]` shows "Puppeteer's" linked to the Puppeteer explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in an interaction text about moving a prisoner to the puppeteer's prison.

label: Puppeteer
summary: The plural name of the game concept Puppeteer ("Puppeteers"), linked to the Puppeteer explanation.
details: In a text, `[puppeteers|E]` shows "Puppeteers" linked to the Puppeteer explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Puppeteer
summary: The plural possessive form of the game concept Puppeteer ("Puppeteers'"), linked to the Puppeteer explanation.
details: In a text, `[puppeteers_possessive|E]` shows "Puppeteers'" linked to the Puppeteer explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Puppet
summary: A verb form of the game concept Puppet ("Puppeting"), linked to the Puppet explanation.
details: In a text, `[puppeting|E]` shows "Puppeting" linked to the Puppet explanation. Vanilla uses it in Christian church situation texts about a secular ruler acting as puppeteer.

label: Puppet
summary: The plural name of the game concept Puppet: characters controlled by a puppeteer.
details: In a text, `[puppets|E]` shows "Puppets" linked to the Puppet explanation. Vanilla uses it in a number of texts, for example texts about votes, the Christian church situation and a decision.

label: Purchase truce
summary: The game concept Purchase Truce: an interaction to buy a truce with another ruler in advance, for gold.
details: In a text, `[purchase_truce_interaction|E]` shows "Purchase Truce" (the interaction's name) linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a struggle text that makes it cheaper.

label: Pursuit
summary: The game concept Pursuit: how many extra losses a victorious army inflicts on the fleeing enemy after a battle.
details: In a text, `[pursuit|E]` shows "Pursuit" linked to the concept's explanation. In the aftermath of a battle, the winner's combined pursuit turns routed enemy soldiers into dead ones. Vanilla uses it in combat and men-at-arms texts.

label: Mandala radiance
summary: A name of the game concept Mandala Radiance ("Radiance"): a mandala ruler's pull for winning and keeping subjects.
details: In a text, `[radiance|E]` shows "Radiance" linked to the Mandala Radiance explanation. It combines the ruler's level of devotion, the level of their mandala capital great building and their mandala aspect level; more radiance brings more subjects and rewards.

label: Mandala radiance
summary: The adjective form of the game concept Mandala Radiance ("Radiant"), linked to the Mandala Radiance explanation.
details: In a text, `[radiant|E]` shows "Radiant" linked to the Mandala Radiance explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a modifier reason ("is radiant").

label: Raid
summary: The game concept Raid: an army raised as raiders plunders a foreign ruler's holding for gold.
details: In a text, `[raid|E]` shows "Raid" linked to the concept's explanation. Raiders are raised at rally points; once they start raiding a holding they stay for a while, then gain gold and loot it. The gold is carried by the army and reaches the treasury only when it gets home.

label: Raid
summary: The icon form of the game concept Raid: it shows the raid icon instead of a word.
details: The concept text for this name is the raid icon. Vanilla writes `[raid_i]` without `|E`, which shows only the icon, in front of values in kurultai council task texts.

label: Raid intent
summary: The game concept Raid Intent: a choice that changes what a raid brings or how the raiding army behaves.
details: In a text, `[raid_intent|E]` shows "Raid Intent" linked to the concept's explanation. Besides the usual gold and prestige, an intent can aim at destroying buildings or capturing characters, or change the army's speed or how much loot it can carry.

label: Raid intent
summary: The plural name of the game concept Raid Intent: choices that change what a raid brings or how the raiders behave.
details: In a text, `[raid_intents|E]` shows "Raid Intents" linked to the Raid Intent explanation. Vanilla uses it in building texts, for example that a building lowers the chance of special intents.

label: Raid
summary: The past form of the game concept Raid ("Raided"), linked to the Raid explanation.
details: In a text, `[raided|E]` shows "Raided" linked to the Raid explanation. Vanilla uses it in message filter texts such as a holding being raided.

label: Raid
summary: A name of the game concept Raid ("Raider"), linked to the Raid explanation.
details: In a text, `[raider|E]` shows "Raider" linked to the Raid explanation. Many vanilla event texts write `raider` as a saved scope instead (`[raider.GetHerHis]`), which is a different thing.

label: Raid
summary: A plural name of the game concept Raid ("Raiders"), linked to the Raid explanation.
details: In a text, `[raiders|E]` shows "Raiders" linked to the Raid explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept texts about raiding armies.

label: Raid
summary: A verb form of the game concept Raid ("Raiding"), linked to the Raid explanation.
details: In a text, `[raiding|E]` shows "Raiding" linked to the Raid explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts, such as kurultai and cultural tradition tooltips.

label: Raid
summary: The plural name of the game concept Raid ("Raids"), linked to the Raid explanation.
details: In a text, `[raids|E]` shows "Raids" linked to the Raid explanation. Vanilla uses it in AI personality and other texts.

label: Rally point
summary: The game concept Rally Point: a gathering place where a ruler's levies and men-at-arms assemble into an army.
details: In a text, `[rally_point|E]` shows "Rally Point" linked to the concept's explanation. In war, soldiers are called up at a rally point; its levies must come from the ruler's own domain or vassals. Rally points can be reorganised, split and merged.

label: Rally point
summary: The plural name of the game concept Rally Point: gathering places where levies and men-at-arms assemble into armies.
details: In a text, `[rally_points|E]` shows "Rally Points" linked to the Rally Point explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept texts such as the one about raids.

label: Diplomatic range
summary: The short name of the game concept Diplomatic Range ("Range"): characters can only interact with others within this range.
details: In a text, `[range|E]` shows "Range" linked to the Diplomatic Range explanation. Neighbouring realms are always in range. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Rank
summary: The game concept Rank: a ruler's place in the game's hierarchy, the personal counterpart of a title's tier.
details: In a text, `[rank|E]` shows "Rank" linked to the concept's explanation. Each title tier has a rank, which limits the highest rank the holder's vassals can have. From top to bottom: hegemon, emperor, king, duke, count, baron.

label: Rank
summary: The plural name of the game concept Rank: rulers' places in the game's hierarchy.
details: In a text, `[ranks|E]` shows "Ranks" linked to the Rank explanation. Vanilla uses it in succession law texts, for example vassals one or two ranks below the title.

label: Artifact rarity
summary: The short name of the game concept Artifact Rarity ("Rarity"): how rare an artifact is.
details: In a text, `[rarity|E]` shows "Rarity" linked to the Artifact Rarity explanation. From lowest to highest the levels are common (the default, never shown), masterwork, famed and illustrious.

label: Realm
summary: The game concept Realm: all the land a ruler controls, directly or through vassals.
details: In a text, `[realm|E]` shows "Realm" linked to the concept's explanation. It differs from the domain, which is only the holdings the ruler owns personally. Vanilla uses it in hundreds of places in the game's texts and interface files.

label: Realm capital
summary: The game concept Realm Capital: the holding where a ruler and their court live.
details: In a text, `[realm_capital|E]` shows "Realm Capital" linked to the concept's explanation. It gives a tax bonus and always passes to the primary heir. Occupying an enemy's realm capital in war gives much war score and sometimes lets the occupier imprison members of the enemy's family.

label: Realm capital
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Realm Capital ("Realm Capital's"), linked to its explanation.
details: In a text, `[realm_capital_possessive|E]` shows "Realm Capital's" linked to the Realm Capital explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Realm capital
summary: The plural name of the game concept Realm Capital: the holdings where rulers and their courts live.
details: In a text, `[realm_capitals|E]` shows "Realm Capitals" linked to the Realm Capital explanation. Vanilla uses it in a cultural tradition text and a puppet action text.

label: Realm heir
summary: The game concept Realm Heir: one of a realm's heirs, who gets all or some of the ruler's titles when the ruler dies.
details: In a text, `[realm_heir|E]` shows "Realm Heir" linked to the concept's explanation. Depending on the succession law a realm has one or several realm heirs. Vanilla uses it in concept texts about heirs.

label: Realm heir
summary: The plural name of the game concept Realm Heir: a realm's heirs, who get the ruler's titles when the ruler dies.
details: In a text, `[realm_heirs|E]` shows "Realm Heirs" linked to the Realm Heir explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept texts about partition.

label: Realm
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Realm ("Realm's"), linked to the Realm explanation.
details: In a text, `[realm_possessive|E]` shows "Realm's" linked to the Realm explanation. Vanilla uses it in the concept text about laws and in decision texts.

label: Realm priest
summary: The game concept Realm Priest: the councillor in charge of religious matters in faiths with the temporal theocracy doctrine.
details: In a text, `[realm_priest|E]` shows "Realm Priest" linked to the concept's explanation. Unlike the court chaplain of lay clergy faiths, the realm priest automatically leases all temple holdings in the ruler's domain and gets part of the taxes and levies of vassal realm priests.

label: Realm priest
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Realm Priest ("Realm Priest's"), linked to its explanation.
details: In a text, `[realm_priest_possessive|E]` shows "Realm Priest's" linked to the Realm Priest explanation. Vanilla uses it in message filter texts about the realm priest's endorsement.

label: Realm priest
summary: The plural name of the game concept Realm Priest: the councillors in charge of religious matters in temporal theocracy faiths.
details: In a text, `[realm_priests|E]` shows "Realm Priests" linked to the Realm Priest explanation. Vanilla uses it in the clergy concept text and in doctrine texts.

label: Realm size
summary: The game concept Realm Size: the number of counties held by a character and their vassals.
details: In a text, `[realm_size|E]` shows "Realm Size" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the core texts and court position salary texts.

label: Realm
summary: The plural name of the game concept Realm: all the land rulers control, directly or through vassals.
details: In a text, `[realms|E]` shows "Realms" linked to the Realm explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts.

label: Rebuilt building
summary: A name of the game concept Rebuilt Building ("Rebuilding"): restoring a ruined building to what it was.
details: In a text, `[rebuilding|E]` shows "Rebuilding" linked to the Rebuilt Building explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a building text about what rebuilding grants.

label: Rebuilt building
summary: A name of the game concept Rebuilt Building ("Rebuilt"): restoring a ruined building to what it was.
details: In a text, `[rebuilt|E]` shows "Rebuilt" linked to the Rebuilt Building explanation. Vanilla uses it in building and great project texts.

label: Rebuilt building
summary: The game concept Rebuilt Building: the act of rebuilding a ruined building, restoring it to its former glory.
details: In a text, `[rebuilt_building|E]` shows "Rebuilt Building" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses it through this name.

label: Recently acquired holding
summary: The game concept Recently Acquired Holding: a holding gained in the last year that put its ruler above their domain limit.
details: Such a holding does not make the ruler's other holdings suffer for being over the limit, but it gives no taxes or levies itself. In a text, `[recently_acquired_holding|E]` shows "Recently Acquired Holding" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the holding view's warning and the realm window's list of these holdings.

label: Recently acquired holding
summary: Another name of the game concept Recently Acquired Holding: a holding gained in the last year that took its ruler over their domain limit.
details: In a text, `[recently_acquired_holdings|E]` shows the plural "Recently Acquired Holdings" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as the heading of the realm window's list of these holdings.

label: Recently disembarked
summary: The game concept Recently Disembarked: the state of an army that has just come ashore after a sea voyage.
details: For a while after landing, the army suffers an advantage penalty in battles. In a text, `[recently_disembarked|E]` shows "Recently Disembarked" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the army's map icon tooltip, with the days left.

label: Reforge artifact
summary: Another name of the game concept Reforge Artifact: turning an inventory artifact into a court artifact.
details: In a text, `[reforge|E]` shows "Reforge" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the antiquarian court position's texts and the artifact durability advice.

label: Reforge artifact
summary: The game concept Reforge Artifact: turning an inventory artifact into a court artifact (one shown in the royal court).
details: It needs an antiquarian at court and costs gold; older artifacts cost less. Reforging also restores the artifact's durability, as a repair does. Only weapons, armor, crowns and regalia can be reforged, and they always become pedestal items. In a text, `[reforge_artifact|E]` shows "Reforge Artifact" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Reformation
summary: Another name of the game concept Reformation: the culture head changing parts of their culture.
details: In a text, `[reform|E]` shows "Reform" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the culture window's reform button tooltip and the culture head's explanation.

label: Reformation
summary: The game concept Reformation: the head of a culture changing some of that culture's parts.
details: What can be changed: traditions, ethos and martial custom. It takes a long time, and once started it cannot be stopped. In a text, `[reformation|E]` shows "Reformation" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in culture explanations and a Kurultai council task's cost text.

label: Refuse conversion
summary: The game concept Refuse Conversion: when refusing a demand to convert counts as a crime.
details: The game lists these conditions for it counting as a crime: the refusing character shares the religion of the one demanding, that religion has heresies, and the demander's faith is hostile or worse towards the refuser's faith. In a text, `[refuse_conversion_crime|E]` shows "Refuse Conversion" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Refuse conversion
summary: Another name of the game concept Refuse Conversion: when refusing a demand to convert counts as a crime.
details: In a text, `[refused_conversion_crime|E]` shows "Refused Conversion" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Refuse conversion
summary: Another name of the game concept Refuse Conversion: when refusing a demand to convert counts as a crime.
details: In a text, `[refusing_conversion_crime|E]` shows "Refusing Conversion" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the Demand Conversion interaction, to say that refusing is a crime.

label: Regency
summary: Another name of the game concept Regency: a diarchy for a ruler who cannot rule on their own.
details: In a text, `[regencies|E]` shows the plural "Regencies" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Regency
summary: Another name of the game concept Regency, in the plural possessive form.
details: In a text, `[regencies_possessive|E]` shows "Regencies'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Regency
summary: The game concept Regency: a special form of diarchy for when the ruler cannot rule the realm on their own.
details: It usually happens when the ruler is a child, imprisoned, incapable, or away at an activity outside the realm. A regency that lasts too long can become an entrenched regency. In a text, `[regency|E]` shows "Regency" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the regent and regent succession score explanations.

label: Regency
summary: Another name of the game concept Regency, in the possessive form.
details: In a text, `[regency_possessive|E]` shows "Regency's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Diarchy veto
summary: The game concept Diarchy Veto: a liege stopping their diarch from using a diarch power.
details: The veto costs the liege prestige. In a text, `[regency_veto|E]` shows "Diarchy Veto" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a concept text as an example next to diarch powers.

label: Regent
summary: The game concept Regent: the name for a diarch during a regency.
details: A ruler can name a regent before a regency starts; otherwise the candidate with the highest regent succession score becomes regent. In a text, `[regent|E]` shows "Regent" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it widely, for example in AI personality and achievement texts.

label: Regent family
summary: The game concept Regent Family: the leading house in a realm that has a ceremonial regent.
details: In a text, `[regent_family|E]` shows "Regent Family" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as a family status in the relations texts.

label: Regent
summary: Another name of the game concept Regent, in the possessive form.
details: In a text, `[regent_possessive|E]` shows "Regent's" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faction reasons (the regent's culture or faith) and in the entrenched regency texts.

label: Regency succession score
summary: The game concept Regency Succession Score: the score that decides which candidate becomes the next regent.
details: The candidate with the highest score is picked, unless the ruler has named a regent, who then goes first. The score favors the ruler's relatives, especially landless family at their court, and politically skilled characters. In a text, `[regent_succession_score|E]` shows "Regency Succession Score" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the regent explanation and a tutorial text.

label: Regent
summary: Another name of the game concept Regent: the diarch during a regency.
details: In a text, `[regents|E]` shows the plural "Regents" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in diarchy and grand wedding texts.

label: Regent
summary: Another name of the game concept Regent, in the plural possessive form.
details: In a text, `[regents_possessive|E]` shows "Regents'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Regiment
summary: The game concept Regiment: a group of soldiers of one type, such as archers, footmen or levies.
details: Levies are organized into regiments too, but the ones that matter most are men-at-arms regiments. In a text, `[regiment|E]` shows "Regiment" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in soldier, counter and achievement texts.

label: Regiment
summary: Another name of the game concept Regiment: a group of soldiers of one type.
details: In a text, `[regiments|E]` shows the plural "Regiments" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in building requirement tooltips about men-at-arms regiments.

label: Region
summary: The game concept Region: a fixed geographical area of the map.
details: Unlike de jure borders, regions never change. In a text, `[region|E]` shows "Region" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in decision texts after a region's name.

label: Region
summary: Another name of the game concept Region: a fixed geographical area of the map.
details: In a text, `[regions|E]` shows "Region" linked to the concept's explanation; the game's text for this plural name is the singular word. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Manually reinforce
summary: The game concept Manually Reinforce: adventurers and nomads must refill their men-at-arms through interactions.
details: Landed rulers' men-at-arms reinforce on their own; adventurers' and nomads' do not, and new recruits have to be won with interactions. In a text, `[reinforce_soldiers|E]` shows "Manually Reinforce" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in government rules and the reinforce interaction's texts.

label: Manually reinforce
summary: Another name of the game concept Manually Reinforce: adventurers and nomads refilling their men-at-arms through interactions.
details: In a text, `[reinforcements|E]` shows "Reinforcements" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in an adventurer perk's effect text.

label: Special relation
summary: The game concept Special Relation: a relationship between characters that is not family or vassalage, such as friend, lover or rival.
details: Relations come in kinds: standard ones (friend, lover, rival, guardian, ward, mentor, student, elder, disciple), upgraded ones (best friend, soulmate, nemesis) and childhood ones (bully, victim, crush). They can carry character modifiers and decide what can happen between the two. In a text, `[relation|E]` shows "Special Relation" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faction reason texts.

label: Special relation
summary: Another name of the game concept Special Relation: a relationship that is not family or vassalage.
details: In a text, `[relations|E]` shows the plural "Special Relations" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept and activity texts.

label: Special relation
summary: Another name of the game concept Special Relation: a relationship that is not family or vassalage.
details: In a text, `[relationship|E]` shows "Special Relationship" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a message filter and diarch succession score texts.

label: Religion
summary: The game concept Religion: a group of related faiths (its denominations).
details: Each religion belongs to one of four religious families: Abrahamic, Eastern, Sinitic or Pagan. In a text, `[religion|E]` shows "Religion" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in many decision texts.

label: Religion
summary: Another name of the game concept Religion: a group of related faiths.
details: In a text, `[religions|E]` shows the plural "Religions" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in war and concept texts.

label: Religious family
summary: Another name of the game concept Religious Family: a group of religions.
details: In a text, `[religious_families|E]` shows the plural "Religious Families" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the religion concept's text.

label: Religious family
summary: The game concept Religious Family: a group of religions that decides how its religions and faiths see each other.
details: For example, the Abrahamic family allows holy wars against everyone, other Abrahamics too, and its religions can have heresies. In a text, `[religious_family|E]` shows "Religious Family" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in requirement texts such as a holder's religious family.

label: Head of faith succession law
summary: The game concept Head of Faith Succession Law: an extra succession law of rulers who are also heads of faith, requiring an heir of the same faith.
details: The law can never be changed, and head of faith titles cannot have their own title succession. It goes away only when an outside force destroys the head of faith title. In a text, `[religious_head_succession_law|E]` shows "Head of Faith Succession Law" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Head of faith succession law
summary: Another name of the game concept Head of Faith Succession Law, in a short form.
details: In a text, `[religious_head_succession_law_short|E]` shows "Head of Faith Law" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as the name of this succession law.

label: Head of faith succession law
summary: Another name of the game concept Head of Faith Succession Law.
details: In a text, `[religious_head_succession_laws|E]` shows "Head of Faith Succession Law" linked to the concept's explanation; the game's text for this plural name is the singular. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Head of faith succession law
summary: Another name of the game concept Head of Faith Succession Law, in a short plural form.
details: In a text, `[religious_head_succession_laws_short|E]` shows "Head of Faith Laws" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Religious relations
summary: The game concept Religious Relations: a council task of the court chaplain.
details: It raises the opinion that theocratic rulers of the same faith have of the character, and raises the character's monthly piety. In a text, `[religious_relations|E]` shows "Religious Relations" (the task's name) linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the task's efficiency text.

label: Religious subordinate
summary: The game concept Religious Subordinate: a character who has a religious superior above them in a religious hierarchy.
details: In a text, `[religious_subordinate|E]` shows "Religious Subordinate" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Religious subordinate
summary: Another name of the game concept Religious Subordinate: a character below a religious superior.
details: In a text, `[religious_subordinates|E]` shows the plural "Religious Subordinates" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a text about asking subordinates for gold.

label: Religious superior
summary: The game concept Religious Superior: a character with religious authority over one or more clergy below them in a religious hierarchy.
details: In a text, `[religious_superior|E]` shows "Religious Superior" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in lists of who counts as a character's clergy, for example next to the court chaplain.

label: Religious superior
summary: Another name of the game concept Religious Superior: a character with religious authority over clergy below them.
details: In a text, `[religious_superiors|E]` shows the plural "Religious Superiors" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Renounce
summary: The game concept Renounce: releasing a prisoner in exchange for them giving up all their claims on titles in your realm.
details: Children of a title's current holder never lose their claims on it while that holder lives. In a text, `[renounce|E]` shows "Renounce" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Renounce
summary: Another name of the game concept Renounce: a prisoner giving up their claims in exchange for release.
details: In a text, `[renounced|E]` shows "Renounced" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it when a prisoner has no claims that can be renounced.

label: Renown
summary: The game concept Renown: prestige that belongs to a whole dynasty instead of one character.
details: A dynasty earns it from its living members, its rulers and its marriages to other rulers; a ruler with a liege of the same dynasty adds none. It raises the dynasty's prestige level, and the dynast spends it on dynasty perks and on influencing members. In a text, `[renown|E]` shows "Renown" linked to the concept's explanation (the concept's own key is `dynasty_prestige`). Vanilla uses it in the dynasty ledger's tooltip.

label: Repair artifact
summary: Another name of the game concept Repair Artifact: paying gold to restore an artifact with low durability.
details: In a text, `[repair|E]` shows "Repair" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in artifact durability advice, next to reforge.

label: Repair artifact
summary: The game concept Repair Artifact: paying gold to restore an artifact whose durability is low.
details: In a text, `[repair_artifact|E]` shows "Repair Artifact" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name; vanilla writes `[repair|E]`.

label: Republic
summary: The game concept Republic: a government form that players cannot play, where an elected citizen rules for life, used by burghers and merchants.
details: Republican vassals have fixed obligations that cannot be changed, so they always give a steady amount of levies and taxes. In a text, `[republic|E]` shows "Republic" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in lists of government forms.

label: Republic
summary: Another name of the game concept Republic: an unplayable government form ruled by an elected citizen.
details: In a text, `[republic_government|E]` shows "Republican Government" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in texts about taxes and levies from republican vassals.

label: Republic
summary: Another name of the game concept Republic that shows its icon.
details: In a text, `[republic_i|E]` shows the republic government icon linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for the republic icon concept.

label: Republic
summary: Another name of the game concept Republic, as the adjective.
details: In a text, `[republican|E]` shows "Republican" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for vassals turned republican.

label: Republic
summary: Another name of the game concept Republic: an unplayable government form ruled by an elected citizen.
details: In a text, `[republics|E]` shows the plural "Republics" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in holding type texts.

label: Request anointment
summary: The game concept Request Anointment: an interaction an emperor-tier or higher ruler uses to ask the head of faith for support in an anointment.
details: When the faith has no head of faith, the ruler asks a clergy head of rite instead. In a text, `[request_anointment|E]` shows "Request Anointment" linked to the concept's explanation (the concept's own key is `anointment_request`). Vanilla uses it to point to the interaction when an anointment is not yet approved.

label: Demand chastity
summary: The game concept Demand Chastity: an interaction that demands another character take vows of chastity.
details: The target gets a long-lasting fertility penalty. In a text, `[request_clerical_chastity_interaction|E]` shows the interaction's name, "Demand Chastity", linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it among the clergy interactions secular rulers may use.

label: Request clerical title expansion
summary: The game concept Request Clerical Title Expansion: an interaction ecclesiastical rulers use to grow their clerical region into the de jure counties of a neighboring duchy.
details: It needs the head of faith's approval. In a text, `[request_ecclesiastical_title_expansion_interaction|E]` shows the interaction's name, "Request Clerical Title Expansion", linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a holy war text about expanding into the target.

label: Research project
summary: The game concept Research Project: an inspiration where the court scholar's aptitude brings benefits to their employer.
details: Rarely, a research project can discover a new innovation. In a text, `[research_project|E]` shows "Research Project" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the court scholar's texts.

label: Research project
summary: Another name of the game concept Research Project: a court scholar's inspiration.
details: In a text, `[research_projects|E]` shows the plural "Research Projects" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.
